meta.title: Who really said "Dedicated to my parents, Ayn Rand and God"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Ayn Rand's words. The serial-comma joke garbles R. M. Bevensee's real 1964 book dedication: "my parents, Ayn Rand, and the glory of GOD."
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Dedicated to my parents, Ayn Rand and God'?
meta.ogDescription: An apocryphal Oxford-comma joke. The genuine 1964 dedication by engineer R. M. Bevensee used the serial comma: "my parents, Ayn Rand, and the glory of GOD."

answer.label: Not Ayn Rand — a garbled 1964 dedication by R. M. Bevensee
answer.authorDates: Assistant Professor of Electrical Engineering, University of California, Berkeley (per his 1964 title page)
answer.sourceLine: The real dedication is in Bevensee’s engineering book Electromagnetic Slow Wave Systems (Wiley, 1964). It reads “my parents, Ayn Rand, and the glory of GOD” and has the serial comma. Quote Investigator ↗ calls the shorter, comma-less “Ayn Rand and God” version apocryphal: a joke made by an unknown person, probably inspired by Bevensee’s page.

source.trailTitle: How a real dedication became a punchline
trail: 1964 — R. M. Bevensee dedicates Electromagnetic Slow Wave Systems to “my parents, / Ayn Rand, / and the glory of GOD”, with the serial comma (scan at Internet Archive ↗).

1997 — A Usenet post to alt.books.reviews, quoted by Quote Investigator, gives “Dedicated to my parents, Ayn Rand and God” as a supposed dedication and adds “Whether apocryphal or not I dunno” (Quote Investigator ↗).
2005 — Richard Lederer’s The Revenge of Anguished English presents “To my parents, Ayn Rand and God” as a real book dedication that argues for the serial comma (cited by Quote Investigator ↗).
2022 — Quote Investigator concludes the comma-less dedication is apocryphal. It suggests Bevensee’s lines inspired an unknown person to write the shorter comic version (read the investigation ↗).
source.cutTag: Popular wording is a joke version
source.excerptNote: In the book the dedication runs over four lines: “This Book is Dedicated to / my parents, / Ayn Rand, / and the glory of GOD”. There is a comma after “Ayn Rand”, so it lists three things, not two parents. The popular “Ayn Rand and God” wording drops that comma and shortens the last item.

author.name: R. M. Bevensee
author.heading: About R. M. Bevensee
author.metaLine: Electrical engineer · author of Electromagnetic Slow Wave Systems (1964)
author.bio: R. M. Bevensee wrote Electromagnetic Slow Wave Systems, a technical monograph published by John Wiley & Sons in 1964. Its title page calls him an Assistant Professor of Electrical Engineering at the University of California, Berkeley. His four-line dedication thanks “my parents, Ayn Rand, and the glory of GOD”. It is the earliest match Quote Investigator found for the famous serial-comma joke.

copyAttribution: “This Book is Dedicated to my parents, Ayn Rand, and the glory of GOD” — R. M. Bevensee, dedication, Electromagnetic Slow Wave Systems (John Wiley & Sons, 1964). The comma-less “Dedicated to my parents, Ayn Rand and God” is an apocryphal joke version, not Ayn Rand’s words (Quote Investigator, 2022).

misattribution.heading: Why Ayn Rand gets the credit
misattribution.intro: This is a grammar joke, not something Ayn Rand said. Her name is in the punchline, so search results and quote sites list her as the author.

items.why: Rand appears only as one of the people being thanked. No source puts the line in her own writing. The first known version is a dedication in another author’s 1964 engineering book (Quote Investigator ↗).

The alt.usage.english FAQ passes on a report that an author who never used the final comma “dedicated a novel” this way (AUE FAQ ↗). The real page is in a technical monograph on electromagnetics, and it does use the serial comma (1964 scan ↗).

items.who: Richard Lederer, The Revenge of Anguished English (2005)
items.why: Lederer offered “To my parents, Ayn Rand and God” as an actual dedication to show why the serial comma matters. Quote Investigator counts it among the places the apocryphal version kept spreading (Quote Investigator ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: The real dedication is R. M. Bevensee’s, from 1964, and it reads “my parents, Ayn Rand, and the glory of GOD” with the serial comma. Quote Investigator judges the comma-less “Ayn Rand and God” version apocryphal (Quote Investigator ↗).

context.heading: Why the joke works, and the irony
lead: Copy editors use the dedication to argue for the serial (Oxford) comma. Without a comma after “Ayn Rand”, the phrase “Ayn Rand and God” can be read as naming the writer’s two parents. The irony is that the real 1964 dedication already had that comma. The ambiguity only appears in the shortened version people retell.

Linguist Laurence Horn joked on the American Dialect Society list that the marriage would be hard, since Rand was “a renowned atheist”. He added that the real “Ayn Rand and the Glory of God” version “is less funny” (ADS-L ↗).
